# zpe-notary

> An append-only public record of file hashes. You publish a hash, sign it, and push. The commit date is the proof
> that the file existed then. No account, no fee, no chain to buy.

## What this is for

A stranger needs to check that a document you show them today is the document you had on a given day. You cannot
prove that with a private file, and a paid notary is slow and does not scale to a page someone links to.

## Records

- `records/<UTC-stamp>.json` - one publication, shaped `zpe.notary.record/1`, with a detached `.sig`.
- `index.json` - every record, its own hash, and how many rows it carries.
- `allowed_signers` - the public keys that sign records, one identity per line.

## Verify a record

```sh
git clone https://github.com/ZPEVC/zpe-notary && cd zpe-notary
ssh-keygen -Y verify -f allowed_signers -I zpe-evidence -n evidence \
  -s records/<record>.json.sig < records/<record>.json
sha256sum your-copy-of-the-file   # must equal the row's sha256
```

## Publish a record

```sh
# rows are {ts, subject, kind, sha256, bytes, source?, method?}
# 1. write records/<UTC-stamp>.json shaped zpe.notary.record/1
# 2. sign it
ssh-keygen -Y sign -f ~/.ssh/your_key -n evidence records/<UTC-stamp>.json
# 3. add your public key to allowed_signers under your own identity
# 4. append the record to index.json
# 5. open a pull request
```

The merge commit is the timestamp that matters.

## What it does not attest

- Not truth. A filing, not a finding.
- Not identity beyond the key that signed.
- Not deletion-proof: a force-push can remove a record from `main`, but every clone keeps the old commit, so a
  disappearance is itself visible.

## Honest limits of the timestamp

GitHub's commit time is a clock we do not run, which is good, and a clock we do not control, which is not the same
as a notary's. If you need an anchor nobody can dispute, add an OpenTimestamps attestation of the record
(`ots stamp records/<record>.json`) and commit the `.ots` file beside it; that anchors the hash in Bitcoin without a
wallet or a fee. Until that exists here, say "GitHub's clock" and not "immutable".

## Why not a blockchain

A timestamp needs one property: nobody can backdate it. A public commit gives that for free. A chain adds a token,
a wallet, gas, and a UX cliff for the person who just wants to check a PDF. If a project needs anchoring into a
chain, OpenTimestamps does it in one file without any of that.

## Why would anyone use this

- A freelancer delivering an audit whose "before" numbers matter.
- An agency publishing a benchmark that a competitor will doubt.
- Anyone selling a report where the client might ask, later, whether the findings were written after the sale.
- A disclosure or a takedown where the date of the notice is the argument.

If you do not make claims someone will doubt, you do not need this. That is most people, and saying so is part of
being trustworthy.
